title: The month of Poh
hookLine: in Poh the frost does not touch the one the Lord embraces (Barah Maha, ang 135)

lines: POH: FOG ON THE FIELDS ALL DAY.
SHAWLS, FIRES, TEA IN BOTH HANDS.
WHO CAN THE FROST NOT TOUCH?
cards: Anyone who has spent winter in a Punjabi village knows the fog. In Poh, roughly mid-December to mid-January, it can sit on the fields all day. The cold gets into the walls.

People wrap up in heavy shawls, sit around small fires, and hand each other cups of tea with both hands. At the very end of the month comes Lohri, a bonfire night when families gather around the flames.
Cold makes you notice warmth. It also makes you notice who is out in it. Guru Arjan's Poh stanza begins in the frost, and asks who it can't touch.

teach.b: The stanza opens pokh tukhaar na vi-aapa-ee, kanth mili-aa har naahu. In paraphrase: in Poh, the frost does not touch the one whom the Lord, the Beloved, has embraced. Tukhaar is frost.
Vi-aapa-ee means to seize, to get into you, the way cold gets into your bones.

teach.h: KANTH MILI-AA: HELD IN AN EMBRACE.
teach.b: Kanth mili-aa is a hug, literally an arm around the neck. So the picture is plain and physical: the cold is real, and you are being held.
The mind is pierced by love for the Lord's lotus feet, and fixed on the sight of Him. Take the shelter of the Lord of the world, it says, and serve the Master; that's the real profit.
And it ends: in Poh, all comforts belong to the one whom the carefree Lord forgives. Notice what it doesn't promise. Winter doesn't go away.

teach.h: THE WEATHER STAYS; THE COLD CAN'T SEIZE.
teach.b: The frost just doesn't seize the one who is embraced: a warmth that works inside the weather. For Sikhs, Poh carries a memory that makes this line hard and holy.
In December, in the early 1700s, Mata Gujri, the mother of Guru Gobind Singh, and his two youngest sons were held at Sirhind in the cold, before the boys were executed.
Tradition remembers they were kept in an open tower in the winter air, and that they did not give up their faith. Many Sikhs gather in Poh to remember them.
Held warm, in the Barah Maha, has never meant nothing hard happens. It means you are not alone in the cold.

how: On the Sangrand of Poh, many gurdwaras read the Poh stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha; in the same season many Sikhs gather to remember Mata Gujri and the younger Sahibzade at Sirhind.

o: deep winter, when frost can't seize the embraced
the bonfire night at the end of winter
a heavy shawl worn against the winter fog

games.q: the month of Poh — tap the pairs.
p: the bonfire night at the end of Poh

s: the Poh stanza promises that winter will go away
it says the frost doesn't seize the one the Lord embraces; the weather stays.
Sikhs remember Mata Gujri and the youngest Sahibzade in this cold season
tradition remembers them held in the winter air at Sirhind.
kanth mili-aa pictures an embrace, an arm around the neck
the warmth in the stanza is the warmth of being held.

games.q: it's the coldest week of the year in Punjab. according to the Poh stanza, who does the frost not touch?
o: the one with the thickest shawl.
the one the Lord has embraced.
the one who stays indoors all month.
games.why: pokh tukhaar na vi-aapa-ee, kanth mili-aa har naahu: in Poh, the frost does not seize the one the Beloved Lord embraces.

practice: Wrap a blanket, a sweater, or just your own arms around yourself, and feel the warmth gather in your shoulders, chest and hands.
Give thanks for it plainly, for the roof, the cloth, the hands that made it, to Waheguru in your own words if you pray, or simply letting gratitude sit in the warmth if you don't.
Spare one breath for someone out in the cold tonight.

wordCard.voice: Poh. In the Barah Maha, Poh is the deep cold, and the frost cannot seize the one the Beloved holds in an embrace.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: tukhaar, frost. In Poh, the stanza says, tukhaar does not seize the one held by the Lord.

carryVoice: Your line: poh: held warm. The cold is real, and so is the embrace. Stay warm; see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Barah Maha, Raag Majh, Mahalla 5, the Poh stanza (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 135)
